Expanding Attention: A Taylor-Series Route to Linear-Time
Transformers with a Fixed Number of Recurrent States

Zicong Huang
October 2026
Abstract

We expand the exponential kernel of attention into a truncated Taylor series of nn terms and factorize each term into a tensor-power inner product, which collapses the causal history into exactly nn recurrent states, each updated by one rank-one outer product per token and independent of context length NN. The recursion is lossless with respect to the truncated kernel (2.2×10−162.2\times 10^{-16} in float64), and the states are additive across chunks (5.7×10−145.7\times 10^{-14}), so prefill admits a parallel scan. Measured exponents are t∝N2.28t\propto N^{2.28} for softmax against N0.91N^{0.91} for states, with a crossover at N≈728N\approx 728 and 20.8×20.8\times at N=8192N=8192; per-token decoding latency is constant at 7.3​μ7.3\,\mus against N1.04N^{1.04} for softmax, giving 76.0×76.0\times at N=65536N=65536. Accuracy improves exponentially in nn while cost grows combinatorially, since the mm-th state is (d+m−1m)\binom{d+m-1}{m} wide—a bound confirmed by SVD—so the optimum is second order, n=3n=3, at 6.5×10−46.5\times 10^{-4} error and 9,9459{,}945 elements per head. Query and key normalization is a prerequisite: without it the argument exceeds the convergence radius and adding terms stops helping.

1 Introduction

The cost of softmax attention is carried by two facts. First, the score matrix is dense: evaluating it costs O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) time and materializing it costs O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) memory. Second, autoregressive decoding must retain every past key and value, so the KV cache grows as O⁡(N)O(N). The present work starts from a single observation: the only nonlinearity that prevents attention from being reordered into a recurrent accumulation is the exponential. Replacing it by a polynomial makes the reordering exact.

Concretely, we write exp⁡(q⊤​k/a)≈∑m=0n−1αm​(q⊤​k)m\exp(q^{\top}k/a)\approx\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}\alpha_{m}(q^{\top}k)^{m} with αm=1/(m!​am)\alpha_{m}=1/(m!\,a^{m}), use the identity (q⊤​k)m=⟨q⊗m,k⊗m⟩(q^{\top}k)^{m}=\langle q^{\otimes m},k^{\otimes m}\rangle, and move the sum over positions inside. What remains is a set of nn matrices, each updated once per token and never revisited. The context length disappears from the memory footprint entirely.

The contribution of this paper is not the algebraic identity, which is elementary and appears in the kernelized-attention literature [1, 5, 6]. The contribution is a measured account of the resulting trade-off: how fast it actually runs, how the running time actually scales, what the truncation order actually costs, and where the construction actually breaks. Every number reported below is a measurement from our own implementation, not a theoretical bound.

2 Related Work

Linear attention. Katharopoulos et al. [1] observed that when the kernel factorizes as κ⁡(q,k)=ϕ​(q)⊤​ϕ​(k)\kappa(q,k)=\phi(q)^{\top}\phi(k), attention can be rewritten as a recurrent accumulation of ϕ⁡(k)​v⊤\phi(k)v^{\top}, giving constant memory and linear time. The choice of feature map ϕ\phi determines both the fidelity of the approximation and the size of the recurrent state.

Feature maps. A variety of maps have been proposed, including the positive random features of Performer [2] and the cosine-based reweighting of cosFormer [3]. Our work is closest to the Taylor expansion of the exponential. Arora et al. [5] adopt a second-order Taylor map, exp⁡(x)≈1+x+x2/2\exp(x)\approx 1+x+x^{2}/2, noting that it expands the recurrent state and improves recall capacity without adding parameters, and report that the map sits on the accuracy–state-size Pareto frontier. Nauen et al. [6] replace the exponential by a Taylor polynomial and unroll the quadratic term with a tensor-product operator, achieving linear complexity, and additionally find that normalizing queries and keys, introducing a per-head temperature, and rescaling the output are needed to prevent training failure from large intermediate norms. Earlier work on higher-order expansions [4] stopped at the quadratic term because of the perceived difficulty of evaluating all polynomial interactions at higher degree.

Higher orders. Recent work revisits higher-degree terms by exploiting the symmetric structure of the tensor powers, showing that the expansion decomposes into symmetric chains of tensor products and that this structure reveals the minimal basis for all polynomial interactions [7]. We reach the same minimal basis (d+m−1m)\binom{d+m-1}{m} from the other direction: we measure the rank of the state matrix directly and show by SVD truncation that this dimension is a hard lower bound rather than an implementation choice.

Relation to this work. We do not propose a new feature map. We take the Taylor map as given and measure what it costs: the actual running time, the actual growth exponent, the actual state width, and the actual failure boundary. Where [5] reports quality at the model level and [6] reports task accuracy, we report numerical deviation from softmax attention, wall-clock scaling, and the rank structure of the state.

3 Method

3.1 Kernel expansion

Let qt,kt∈ℝdq_{t},k_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the query and key at position tt, let vt∈ℝdvv_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} be the value, let NN be the context length, let nn be the number of retained Taylor terms, and let aa be a temperature constant. Causal attention is

ot=∑i≤texp⁡(qt⊤​ki/a)​vi∑i≤texp⁡(qt⊤​ki/a).o_{t}\;=\;\frac{\sum_{i\leq t}\exp\!\big(q_{t}^{\top}k_{i}/a\big)\,v_{i}}{\sum_{i\leq t}\exp\!\big(q_{t}^{\top}k_{i}/a\big)}. (1)

Truncating the exponential at nn terms gives the polynomial kernel

exp⁡(q⊤​ka)≈∑m=0n−1αm​(q⊤​k)m,αm=1m!​am.\exp\!\left(\frac{q^{\top}k}{a}\right)\;\approx\;\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}\alpha_{m}\,(q^{\top}k)^{m},\qquad\alpha_{m}=\frac{1}{m!\,a^{m}}. (2)

3.2 Decoupling positions from the kernel

The step that removes NN is the tensor-power factorization

(q⊤​k)m=⟨q⊗m,k⊗m⟩,q⊗m=q⊗⋯⊗q⏟m​times.(q^{\top}k)^{m}\;=\;\big\langle q^{\otimes m},\;k^{\otimes m}\big\rangle,\qquad q^{\otimes m}=\underbrace{q\otimes\cdots\otimes q}_{m\ \text{times}}. (3)

Substituting Eq. (3) into Eq. (2) and then into Eq. (1), the sum over ii no longer involves qtq_{t}, so it can be accumulated incrementally. Define, for each order mm,

Sm​(t)=∑i≤tki⊗m⊗vi,Tm​(t)=∑i≤tki⊗m,S_{m}(t)\;=\;\sum_{i\leq t}k_{i}^{\otimes m}\otimes v_{i},\qquad T_{m}(t)\;=\;\sum_{i\leq t}k_{i}^{\otimes m}, (4)

so that

ot=∑m=0n−1αm​⟨qt⊗m,Sm​(t)⟩∑m=0n−1αm​⟨qt⊗m,Tm​(t)⟩.o_{t}\;=\;\frac{\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}\alpha_{m}\big\langle q_{t}^{\otimes m},S_{m}(t)\big\rangle}{\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}\alpha_{m}\big\langle q_{t}^{\otimes m},T_{m}(t)\big\rangle}. (5)

3.3 Exactly nn states, not 2​n2n

Equation (4) appears to require two states per order. It does not. Augment the value with a constant coordinate,

v~i=[vi1]∈ℝdv+1,Am​(t)=∑i≤tki⊗m⊗v~i.\tilde{v}_{i}\;=\;\begin{bmatrix}v_{i}\\ 1\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}+1},\qquad A_{m}(t)\;=\;\sum_{i\leq t}k_{i}^{\otimes m}\otimes\tilde{v}_{i}. (6)

The first dvd_{v} rows of AmA_{m} are SmS_{m} and the last row is TmT_{m}. A single rank-one update

Am​(t)=Am​(t−1)+kt⊗m⊗v~tA_{m}(t)\;=\;A_{m}(t-1)\;+\;k_{t}^{\otimes m}\otimes\tilde{v}_{t} (7)

therefore feeds numerator and denominator simultaneously. The model stores exactly nn states, and each costs O⁡(dm​(dv+1))O\big(d^{m}(d_{v}+1)\big) per token, independent of tt. Nothing is ever recomputed from the beginning of the sequence; the recursion is the algorithm.

3.4 The states are narrower than dmd^{m}

The tensor k⊗mk^{\otimes m} is symmetric, so its dmd^{m} entries contain only (d+m−1m)\binom{d+m-1}{m} distinct monomials. Writing the state in this symmetric minimal basis, with multiplicity corrections cι=m!/∏ici!c_{\iota}=\sqrt{m!/\prod_{i}c_{i}!}, preserves the inner product exactly: ⟨ϕm​(q),ϕm​(k)⟩=(q⊤​k)m\langle\phi_{m}(q),\phi_{m}(k)\rangle=(q^{\top}k)^{m}. We confirm the dimension empirically in Section 5.4: the span of {k⊗m}\{k^{\otimes m}\} over 2,0002{,}000 random keys saturates at rank exactly (d+m−1m)\binom{d+m-1}{m}.

3.5 Chunked evaluation

As in [5], we split the computation into an on-diagonal part, a c×cc\times c quadratic block that is masked causally and costs a constant independent of NN, and an off-diagonal part handled by the nn linear states. States are additive across chunks, as verified in Section 5.2, so chunks may be processed in parallel and their states summed.

4 Complexity

Time. Prefill costs O⁡(N​∑m(d+m−1m)⁡(dv+1))O\big(N\sum_{m}\binom{d+m-1}{m}(d_{v}+1)\big) for the state part plus O⁡(N​c​d)O(Ncd) for the diagonal blocks; both are linear in NN. Softmax attention costs O⁡(N2​d)O(N^{2}d).

Decoding. One token costs O⁡(∑m(d+m−1m)⁡(dv+1))O\big(\sum_{m}\binom{d+m-1}{m}(d_{v}+1)\big) for the state model, a constant, against O⁡(N​d)O(Nd) for softmax, which must rescan the entire cache.

Memory. The state model stores ∑m=0n−1(d+m−1m)⁡(dv+1)\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}\binom{d+m-1}{m}(d_{v}+1) numbers, independent of NN. The KV cache stores N⁡(d+dv)N(d+d_{v}) numbers and grows without bound.

5 Experiments

Unless stated otherwise: d=16d=16, dv=64d_{v}=64, a=2.0a=2.0, chunk size c=256c=256, float32, single-threaded NumPy on CPU. Queries and keys are row-normalized to the unit sphere; Section 5.9 shows this is mandatory. Reference outputs come from causally masked softmax attention with the same aa. Timings are the minimum of repeated runs.

5.1 Is the recursion lossless?

We compare the recurrent state formulation against an explicitly materialized N×NN\times N truncated-kernel attention, in float64 with d=6d=6, dv=4d_{v}=4, N=64N=64, a=da=\sqrt{d}.

Agreement is at machine precision for every order tested. The recurrence does not approximate the truncated-kernel computation; it is that computation, reordered.

5.2 Additivity and parallel scan

Chunk-parallel prefill requires state additivity. Building states on [0,32)[0,32) and [32,64)[32,64) separately and summing them reproduces the state built on [0,64)[0,64) to 5.684×10−145.684\times 10^{-14}, and the resulting outputs agree to 1.665×10−161.665\times 10^{-16}.

5.3 Does one really avoid recomputation?

We compare the recurrence against a baseline that, at every step tt, rescans all of 1,…,t1,\ldots,t. Outputs agree to 4.441×10−164.441\times 10^{-16}. Their scaling differs sharply, as shown in Table 2.

Growth per doubling is about 2×2\times for the recurrence against about 3.4×3.4\times for rescanning. Short sequences favour rescanning only because of the Python-loop constant overhead in this particular implementation; the asymptotic separation is unmistakable.

5.4 State width: (d+m−1m)\binom{d+m-1}{m}, and it is a hard bound

This dimension is a lower bound, not an implementation artifact. Truncating the order-22 state to rank rr by SVD, with d=6d=6 and dv=24d_{v}=24, gives Table 4.

5.5 Growth rate

Fitting t∝Nαt\propto N^{\alpha} over NN from 512512 to 81928192 gives α=2.28\alpha=2.28 for softmax and α=0.91\alpha=0.91 for the state model, matching the theoretical 22 and 11. See Table 5.

The fitted crossover sits at N≈728N\approx 728. Extrapolating both fitted lines beyond the measured range gives Table 6; these entries are not measurements and are included only to show where the gap opens.

5.6 Decoding: constant against linear

This is where the advantage is largest. Table 7 reports per-token latency with the state model’s states prebuilt.

The state model is flat at about 7.3​μ7.3\,\mus across a 64×64\times change in context length, while softmax latency grows linearly.

5.7 Effect of the truncation order

Table 8 sweeps the order at fixed N=2048N=2048, d=16d=16, dv=64d_{v}=64, with a softmax baseline of 32.7 ms.

Two regimes are visible. Accuracy improves exponentially in nn: each extra term divides the error by roughly 1010 to 1818. Cost grows combinatorially: each extra order multiplies the state width by 44 to 99 at d=16d=16, because (d+m−1m)\binom{d+m-1}{m} runs 1,16,136,816,3,876,15,5041,16,136,816,3{,}876,15{,}504. The result is a sharp optimum at n=3n=3, that is, second order: error 6.5×10−46.5\times 10^{-4} at 9,9459{,}945 elements per head, whereas n=4n=4 buys only about 18×18\times more accuracy for 6.3×6.3\times the state and 14×14\times the time.

5.8 State size against head dimension and order

Table 9 reports state size at bf16 with dv=64d_{v}=64, where K denotes KB and M denotes MB.

For comparison, the KV cache at d=16d=16 and dv=64d_{v}=64 is 0.6 MB at N=4,096N=4{,}096, 5.0 MB at N=32,768N=32{,}768, and 20.0 MB at N=131,072N=131{,}072, and it keeps growing while the state does not. Head dimension is the real switch: at d=64d=64 the six-term model needs 1.4 GB per head and is simply infeasible, while at d=16d=16 it costs 2.5 MB.

5.9 Convergence radius: normalization is mandatory

Table 10 reports relative error against causal softmax with d=8d=8, dv=8d_{v}=8, N=96N=96.

Without normalization the argument reaches 5.575.57 and adding terms stops helping: the error at n=6n=6 is 1.43×10−11.43\times 10^{-1}, worse than the 1.09×10−11.09\times 10^{-1} at n=5n=5. Under a more aggressive temperature of a=0.5a=0.5, where the mean of |x/a||x/a| reaches 3.593.59, the truncated series diverges outright. Normalizing qq and kk to the unit sphere and using a=2a=2 restores clean exponential convergence.

5.10 Signed weights from truncation

A truncated polynomial is no longer positive. The fraction of negative kernel entries, measured with d=6d=6, N=64N=64, a=da=\sqrt{d}, is 13.7%13.7\% for n=2n=2, 0.0%0.0\% for n=3n=3, 5.2%5.2\% for n=4n=4, and 0.0%0.0\% for n=5n=5: stopping at an even highest order avoids negative weights. The failure mode is most vivid on the negative axis, where the polynomial departs from exp\exp in both magnitude and sign, as shown in Table 11.

At x=−4x=-4 the first-order truncation returns −3-3 where the true value is 0.0180.018. Normalization, Section 5.9, keeps the operating range away from this region in practice.

6 Discussion

Where the speed comes from. Not from a better constant, but from the exponent: N0.91N^{0.91} against N2.28N^{2.28} in prefill, and N0.00N^{0.00} against N1.04N^{1.04} in decoding. The decoding number is the practically decisive one, because generation is where the KV cache is felt.

The order is a trade, not a dial. Section 5.7 shows exponential accuracy gains against combinatorial cost growth. Because the error already reaches 6.5×10−46.5\times 10^{-4} at n=3n=3, higher orders mostly buy state size. This matches the independent choice of a second-order map with a small head dimension in [5].

Two prerequisites. Queries and keys must be normalized so that |q⊤​k/a|≲1|q^{\top}k/a|\lesssim 1, Section 5.9, and the truncation should stop at an even highest order to avoid negative weights, Section 5.10. Under both, the method is well behaved. The first prerequisite is consistent with the normalization scheme that [6] found necessary for training stability, which suggests the requirement is not an artifact of our random-input setup.

Limitations. All measurements are single-threaded NumPy on CPU with random synthetic qq, kk, and vv; the absolute millisecond figures will not transfer to a GPU, although the fitted exponents reflect the algorithms and should. The projection down to d=16d=16 that is required to keep state size manageable is not modeled here and carries an unmeasured expressivity cost. No language-modeling perplexity or downstream task is evaluated; accuracy is reported only as deviation from softmax attention on random inputs.

7 Conclusion

Expanding the exponential kernel into nn Taylor terms turns the O⁡(N)O(N) KV cache into nn fixed-size recurrent states. We confirmed numerically that the resulting recursion is exact with respect to the truncated kernel, to about 10−1610^{-16}; that the states are additive and therefore parallelizable; and that the growth exponents are 0.910.91 and 0.000.00 for prefill and decoding, against 2.282.28 and 1.041.04 for softmax, yielding 20.8×20.8\times at N=8192N=8192 and 76.0×76.0\times per token at N=65,536N=65{,}536. The optimal operating point is second order, n=3n=3, with a small head dimension, provided queries and keys are normalized.
